issue_context.title: [2.0 RC2] Ado.Net reminders provider is broken in RC2
issue_context.body:
After upgrade to RC2 I have exception when using Ado.Net reminders provider. I configure it as:

```
        .UseAdoNetReminderService(options =>
         {
                 options.ConnectionString = ConnectionString;
                 options.Invariant = "System.Data.SqlClient";
          })
```

and on `_siloHost = builder.Build();` I got: 
```
Orleans.Runtime.OrleansConfigurationException
  HResult=0x80131500
  Message=Invalid AdoNetReminderTableOptions values for AdoNetReminderTable. Invariant is required.
  Source=Orleans.Reminders.AdoNet
  StackTrace:
   at Orleans.Configuration.AdoNetReminderTableOptionsValidator.ValidateConfiguration()
   at Orleans.Hosting.SiloHostBuilder.ValidateSystemConfiguration(IServiceProvider serviceProvider)
   at Orleans.Hosting.SiloHostBuilder.Build()
   at <....>.Orleans.Start() in <....>\Orelans.cs:line 53
   at <....>.Program.Service.Start() in <....>\Program.cs:line 28
   at <....>.Program.<>c.<Main>b__1_3(Service tc) in <....>\Program.cs:line 53
   at Topshelf.ServiceConfiguratorExtensions.<>c__DisplayClass2_0`1.<WhenStarted>b__0(T service, HostControl control)
   at Topshelf.Builders.DelegateServiceBuilder`1.DelegateServiceHandle.Start(HostControl hostControl)
   at Topshelf.Hosts.ConsoleRunHost.Run()

```

review_comments: This is not required, is it? Is there a reason why being explicit is better here? Not pushing back, just commenting, as I don't necessarily find it better (unless it was required to compile to the right thing)
It's not required, I decided it's better to be explicit here
wow this is dangerous mistake which really easy to miss, since it doesn't have compile time validation. I wonder do we make the same mistake in our other part of code base..

how do we find a way to solve the ambiguous between `Action<TOptions>` and `Action<OptionsBuilder<TOptions>>`. If we are making this mistake, our users would probably make the same mistake somewhere else.. @sergeybykov @BenjaminGibbs @jason-bragg @jdom
The PR LGTM, but just want to bring up this issue.
yep :) thanks for pointing this out. And apologize to the other Ben. But welcome to leave feedback if you want :)

I'm trying to find places where end-users would use the wrong signature too, but can'd think of any. It's not common to define a method that takes and OptionsBuilder, only infrastructure code like ours or 3rd party extensions would do this, to provide syntactic sugar for the end user. End users would just either use our extension methods or call `.Configure(Action<TOptions>)` and not use the builder itself.  Still, this is the API for Options, not Orleans, not much we should do if it was an issue (which I still don't believe it is).
I ran a regex search and didn't find any other issues.

Yeah the only thing which bothered me as an user, is when both has defaults to null . For example : 
```
UseXXX(Action<TOptions> configure = null);
UseXXX(Action<OptionBuilder<TOptions>> configure = null)
```

As a user, if I want to call `UseXXX()` I will have to cast it somehow to determine which one. I definitly encounterred this before when writting tests, not sure if there's still occurence like this in our code base 

This is not a OptionsBuilder specific issue. But c# specific. But I point it out because we normally have both overrides for `Action<TOptions> ` and `Action<OptionBuilder<TOptions>> ` and sometimes we forgot it will be an issue if we give both default values,
Yes, we should be consistent with our APIs - no ambiguities. Only the `Action<T>` overload should have a default value in my opinion. Someone can change those things in another PR
yeah totally. I didn't intend to push those in this PR. it just triggered my thought. This pr is good.
I can merge it if tests are passing in vso. @sergeybykov mentioned they weren't
oh, sorry, just read this last comment. Nevertheless I did check that a newer VSO build was passing before merging
I should have updated the thread to say that the tests were passing - my bad.
